title: Grade Calculator
story: Report card day! You got an 87 on your math test. Is that an A? A B? Your teacher uses a scale: 90+ is A, 80+ is B, 70+ is C, 60+ is D, below 60 is F. Let's write a program that takes any score and instantly tells you the letter grade!
why: Many real-world systems use tiered categories � grades, shipping rates, tax brackets, loyalty levels. `elif` chains handle these cleanly by checking conditions from highest to lowest.
analogy: An elif chain is like a prize ladder � you start at the top tier, and if you don't qualify, you drop down to the next tier, until you either win a prize or reach the bottom.
expected_output:
Your score:
87
Grade: B � Great work!
Another score:
45
Grade: F
try_it: Test with different scores: 95, 82, 71, 60, 45. Do you get the right grades? Then create your own elif chain for a different topic: movie ratings (G, PG, PG-13, R) based on age, or T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) based on a number measurement.
tips: Always order `elif` conditions from highest to lowest (or lowest to highest) � never mix directions.
Only the FIRST matching condition runs � later conditions are skipped even if they would also be true.
The final `else` catches everything that didn't match any condition above it.
You can have as many `elif` blocks as you need � 3, 5, even 10 if the problem requires it.
common_mistakes: Writing conditions in random order: `if score >= 60` before `elif score >= 90` means the A-grade check never runs.
Writing `else if` instead of `elif` � XIOM uses the shorter `elif` keyword.
Putting a condition on the final `else`: `else score < 60 {` is wrong � `else` doesn't take a condition.
Forgetting that boundaries matter: `score >= 90` for A means 89 gets a B. If you write `score > 90` for A, then exactly 90 gets a B.
